04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma had been tempted to treat the dispatch ledger as the point where the foundation's procedures met reality. On reflection it marked only an intermediate step. An entry recording dispatch could be accurate while the intended recipient remained unaware of the decision, and the fourteen-day review period made that distinction potentially consequential.

Fiona Bell's next email contained a page from a 2011 office manual headed “Returned correspondence”. It directed staff, when post came back undelivered, to verify the address, attempt renewed contact and document the action taken. The instructions were unremarkable; the uncertainty lay in whether and when they had been applied.

Emma asked Fiona whether any completed returns log or follow-up notes had survived. Fiona could confirm neither. She also cautioned that the manual dealt specifically with mail returned to the office. It did not address the more elusive possibility of a letter going astray without being returned.

“The procedure might have worked perfectly,” Sarah observed when Emma explained.

“It might. But its existence cannot substitute for a record of what actually happened.”

Nor could the absence of such a record demonstrate neglect. Emma requested an inventory-level account of any surviving returns documentation, avoiding names or addresses. A count, if responsibly derived, would be more useful than an intrusive search for a particular applicant.

An unexpected lead came from the newspaper archive. Staff were not prepared to release unpublished correspondence from 2011, but an archivist offered to search a subject index whose entries summarised the material held. The index was not a transcript. Its headings might have been supplied by an editor rather than by the original writers.

In the afternoon a single description emerged: an October 2011 item indexed as “Student Travel — decision not received”. No author was disclosed, and the underlying letter remained unavailable.

Sarah interpreted it immediately as testimony from a student whose appeal rights had been frustrated. Emma disagreed with the certainty, not the possibility. The heading did not identify a student, establish what decision was awaited or reveal whether any review deadline had expired. It could even describe a question about communication rather than an allegation of failed delivery.

The temptation to connect it to the parent's September complaint was equally strong. Yet two documents concerning dissatisfaction with the same scheme were not automatically from the same household. Emma kept their provenance separate.

She entered the October reference in her research log exactly as supplied, including the archivist's warning about the index. Then she checked Fiona's latest reply. No returns log had yet been confirmed, and the manual offered no general reminder system for applicants who did not acknowledge receipt. Both details were potentially relevant, neither decisive.

Emma had previously written three stages across her notebook: Prepared, Dispatched, Received. Now she added Able to seek review. That final condition was not merely administrative. Even confirmed delivery could not by itself show that a recipient understood the decision, the fourteen-day limit or the procedure for challenging it.

The anonymous caller's instructions about payments suddenly seemed remote. The financial questions still mattered, but the documents were directing Emma towards a different uncertainty: whether a formal opportunity to challenge a decision had been meaningful in practice.

She closed the file without drafting a headline. Her next request would be to the archive, asking what could be verified about the October entry without exposing the writer. Only then might she begin to distinguish a communication failure from a misleading label.
